M2.S5.T5.C27.name: Isosceles Right Triangles, Q3
M2.S5.T5.C27.q: The hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle is 10. What are its other two sidelengths? [Hint: Find the area of the square composed of two such right triangles.]
steps: Two such triangles make a square whose diagonal is the hypotenuse, 10.
The square on the hypotenuse has area 10 × 10 = 100.
The square made of the two triangles has half that area: 100 ÷ 2 = 50.
Its side is an equal side of the triangle, so each equal side is √50.
M2.S5.T5.C27.ans: Each of the other two sides is √50, between 7.07 and 7.08

M3.S7.T7.C36.name: Chapter Exercises, Q7
M3.S7.T7.C36.q: Construct a square whose area is equal to the difference of the areas of squares of sidelengths 5 units and 7 units.
steps: The areas are 7² = 49 and 5² = 25, and 49 − 25 = 24.
Draw a side of 5 units, a right angle at one end, and swing an arc of radius 7 from the other end to meet the perpendicular: a right triangle with hypotenuse 7 and one side 5.
Its third side b has b² = 7² − 5², which is 24.
The square on that third side has area 24 square units.
M3.S7.T7.C36.ans: The square on the third side of the right triangle with hypotenuse 7 and one side 5: area 24 square units

M3.S9.T9.C40.name: Missing Sides and New Squares, Q2
M3.S9.T9.C40.q: If a right-angled triangle has a short side of length 8 cm and hypotenuse of length 17 cm, what is the length of the third side? Again, try drawing the triangle and measuring, and then check your answer using Baudhāyana's Theorem.
steps: Draw a side of 8 cm, a right angle at one end, and swing an arc of 17 cm from the other end; the third side measures about 15 cm.
The hypotenuse is given, so subtract.
15² = 225, so the third side is 15.

M3.S9.T9.C41.name: Missing Sides and New Squares, Q4 (i)
M3.S9.T9.C41.q: Let a, b and c denote the length of the sides of a right triangle, with c being the length of the hypotenuse. Find the missing sidelength in each of the following cases: (i) a = 5, b = 7

M3.S9.T9.C42.name: Chapter Exercises, Q2 (a)
M3.S9.T9.C42.q: Find the missing sidelengths in the following right triangles: (a) a tilted right triangle with sides 7 and 9 at the right angle.
steps: The right angle is between the sides 7 and 9, so the missing side faces it: the hypotenuse.

M3.S9.T9.C43.name: Chapter Exercises, Q4
M3.S9.T9.C43.q: Is the hypotenuse the longest side of a right triangle? Justify your answer.
steps: In a right triangle, c² = a² + b².
b² is more than 0, so c² is more than a², and so c is more than a.
In the same way c² is more than b², so c is more than b.
So the hypotenuse is longer than each of the other two sides.
M3.S9.T9.C43.ans: Yes: c² = a² + b² is bigger than a² and bigger than b², so c is the longest side

M3.S11.T11.C57.name: Triples, Q2
M3.S11.T11.C57.q: Does this method yield non-primitive Baudhāyana triples? [Hint: Observe that among the triples generated, one of the smaller sidelengths is one less than the hypotenuse.]
steps: Every triple from the method has the form (the root of the odd square, n − 1, n).
Any common factor of n − 1 and n also divides their difference, which is 1.
So n − 1 and n share no factor greater than 1, and neither can the whole triple.
M3.S11.T11.C57.ans: No: every triple the method gives is primitive

M3.S11.T11.C58.name: Triples, Q3
M3.S11.T11.C58.q: Are there primitive triples that cannot be obtained through this method? If yes, give examples.
steps: The method gives only triples in which the hypotenuse is 1 more than a side.
In none of them is the hypotenuse 1 more than a side, so the method misses them.

M3.S11.T11.C59.name: Chapter Exercises, Q5
M3.S11.T11.C59.q: True or False: Every Baudhāyana triple is either a primitive triple or a scaled version of a primitive triple.
steps: Take any triple (a, b, c) and let f be the greatest common factor of a, b and c.
If f = 1, the triple is primitive.
If f is more than 1, then (a/f, b/f, c/f) is a triple with no common factor greater than 1: a primitive triple.
And (a, b, c) is f times that primitive triple: a scaled version.

M3.S11.T11.C60.name: Chapter Exercises, Q6
M3.S11.T11.C60.q: Give 5 examples of rectangles whose sidelengths and diagonals are all integers.
steps: The diagonal of a rectangle is the hypotenuse of the right triangle made by two of its sides.
So the two sides and the diagonal must form a Baudhāyana triple.

M4.S14.T14.C65.name: Chapter Exercises, Q8 (i)
M4.S14.T14.C65.q: Using the dots of a grid as the vertices, can you create a square that has an area of (a) 2 sq. units, (b) 3 sq. units, (c) 4 sq. units, and (d) 5 sq. units?
steps: A square with its corners on grid dots has a side that goes p dots across and q dots up, so its area is p² + q².
(a) p = 1, q = 1: 1² + 1² = 2, a tilted square of area 2.
(c) p = 2, q = 0: an upright 2 by 2 square, area 4.
(d) p = 1, q = 2: 1² + 2² = 5, a tilted square of area 5.
(b) 3 is not a sum of two squares: 0 + 1, 1 + 1, 0 + 4 and 1 + 4 give 1, 2, 4 and 5, never 3.
M4.S14.T14.C65.ans: Yes for areas 2, 4 and 5; no square of area 3 is possible

M4.S14.T14.C66.name: Chapter Exercises, Q9
M4.S14.T14.C66.q: Find the area of an equilateral triangle with sidelength 6 units. [Hint: Show that an altitude bisects the opposite side. Use this to find the height.]
steps: Drop the altitude from the top vertex to the base; it makes two right triangles.
They have equal hypotenuses (6), the altitude in common and right angles, so they are congruent and the altitude bisects the base into 3 and 3.
In one right triangle: 6² − 3² = 36 − 9 = 27, so h² = 27 and h = √27.
Area = 1/2 × base × height = 1/2 × 6 × √27, which is 3√27.
